turns.name: P1-intro
turns.question: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: who used it, what problem, where my responsibility started and ended
card.say: The users were travelers on the KKday app. Planning a trip by hand was slow: they worked out the budget, searched products one by one, then put the plan together themselves. My responsibility started at the technical plan. I designed the agent, connected it to our product and order data, and built the core backend. It ended at the Android side of the result.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer's follow-up on this project.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names real users (KKday travelers), the problem (manual trip planning), and the candidate's scope (technical plan, agent design, backend, ending at Android side), with no invented employers, titles, or numbers.
judge.criterion: SAY introduces one real Android project from the candidate's background with its users, the problem and the candidate's own scope; no invented employers, titles or numbers.

turns.name: P1-dyn
turns.question: On the KKday agent project, you said your responsibility "ended at the Android side" — so which exact pieces did you build yourself versus the team?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: which exact pieces I built myself versus the team
card.say: I built the agent design and the core backend myself. That covers the tools for product and order data, the personalization data layer, and the checks with retry and fallback. On Android, I wrote the code that reads the SSE stream of the trip plan. The app team built the other screens, like the day cards and the map. The project had five people, and I was the technical lead.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer's follow-up on this project.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer specifies what the candidate built (agent design, core backend, SSE stream reader) versus the team (day cards, map screens), which follows from and adds detail beyond the earlier "ended at the Android side" statement. It stays consistent with the earlier claim of designing the agent and building the core backend, is technically plausible, and introduces no invented employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-change
turns.question: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: pick one change I personally made, walk one user action through the path
card.say: The change I made myself is the Android side of the trip plan stream. A user types "Tokyo, 5,000 yuan, 3 days" and taps plan. The app opens the SSE connection and reads each event as it arrives. I parse each event into a day card and post it to a StateFlow, so the screen shows day one while the rest is still coming. The logic I changed is the parsing and the state update, not the screens.
card.then: Next I'd cover what happens when the stream breaks or an event fails the checks.

more: The parsing runs on a background dispatcher, so the main thread only updates the UI. Each event is checked before it becomes a card. If one event is bad, I skip it and keep the rest of the plan.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer traces a user action (typing a trip request and tapping plan) through concrete layers — SSE network connection, event parsing, StateFlow state update, and UI day cards — and names the changed logic (parsing and state update, not the screens). It separates own work (Android stream parsing) from the team's (screens like day cards and map), and contains no invented numbers.
judge.criterion: SAY traces one user action through concrete layers (UI, state, data or network) and says which logic the candidate changed; separates own work from the team's; no invented numbers.

turns.name: P2-bug
turns.question: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: hardest bug to reproduce, what I suspected, what proved me wrong
card.say: The hardest one was a plan that looked fine but showed the wrong day order. I first suspected the stream itself, so I logged every event as it arrived. The log showed the events came in order, so the stream was fine. The real cause was my own parsing: I keyed the cards by arrival, not by the day number in the event. So a late retry from the backend put day two above day one.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a clear timeline — first suspicion (the stream), the evidence that overturned it (logging every event showed they arrived in order), and the root cause (keying cards by arrival rather than day number), with observations (log output) distinguished from conclusions (stream was fine, real cause was parsing).
judge.criterion: SAY gives a timeline: first suspicion, the evidence (log, experiment or repro) that overturned it, and the root cause, distinguishing observation from conclusion.

turns.name: P2-dyn
turns.question: You said a late retry from the backend put day two above day one — how did you confirm that was the actual cause rather than just a plausible story?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: how did you confirm the cause, not just a plausible story
card.say: I reproduced it on purpose. I sent the same plan again with a late day-two event, and the cards came out in the wrong order every time. Then I changed the key to the day number, and the same replay came out in order. That proved it was my parsing, not the stream.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer adds a concrete repro (replaying the plan with a late day-two event) and a confirming fix (keying by day number), which follows from the earlier parsing-cause explanation, stays consistent with the candidate's Android/SSE role, and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-alt
turns.question: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: other options, why not them, how did you know it worked after release
card.say: There were two other options. First, I could sort the cards on the screen after each update. That works, but the list jumps around while the user is reading. Second, I could ask the backend to send the days in order and wait for the full plan. That's slower, and a late retry can still arrive out of order.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names two real alternatives (sorting on screen, backend ordering) with the constraint that ruled each out (list jumping, slower plus late retries still out of order), and it gives the source of the result (a deliberate replay test with a late day-two event, then re-checking after the key change) — though it does not state the limits of that evidence, the criterion's examples are covered correctly and nothing is said wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY names a real alternative and the constraint that ruled it out, and the source of the result (metric, test, ticket or feedback) with its limits.

turns.name: P3-risk
turns.question: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?

card.problem: Tell about a delivery risk where the team disagreed: when I told whom, options, who decided, what I finished
card.heard: a delivery risk where the team disagreed
card.say: At KKday, close to a release, I found that some old pages broke the back button with the new navigation. I hadn't checked every page yet, but it could already affect the release. I told the project manager that same day. I gave two options: keep the old pages and move my change to the next release, or ship it and accept the risk. He decided to move my change.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a concrete case (back-button breakage near release), says when (same day) and whom (project manager) was told, offers two options, names the PM as decision-maker, and attributes it to KKday.
judge.criterion: SAY describes one concrete case: when and whom the candidate told, the options offered, who had the decision, and what the candidate personally did; attributes the case to the right company.

turns.name: P3-dyn
turns.question: You said the PM chose to "move my change" rather than ship with the back-button risk — so what risk were you personally willing to accept before that release, and what signal afterward would have made you pause or roll back?

card.problem: Tell about a delivery risk where the team disagreed: when I told whom, options, who decided, what I finished
card.heard: what risk I'd accept, what signal would make me pause or roll back
card.say: Before that release, I was willing to accept one risk: the pages I hadn't checked yet might also break. So I said that clearly, and I asked for a quick way to turn the new navigation off. After release, I watched the crash reports and the back-button errors in Bugly. If the number went up, I'd pause the change and keep the old pages working. Then I'd own the fix and the retest, and we'd ship it again when the errors were gone.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer adds specifics (a kill switch for the new navigation, watching crash reports and back-button errors in Bugly, pausing and rolling back if errors rose) that follow from the earlier back-button risk story, stay consistent with the candidate's role and KKday context, and invent no new employer, title, or metric.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W1-scope
turns.question: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.heard: design a mobile wallet, start by clarifying requirements, which user path is the MVP
card.say: Before I design anything, I'd like to confirm a few things. Who are the users: friends sending money to each other, or a business paying customers? Where does the money actually live: a real bank or card behind the wallet, or a stored balance we hold ourselves? And what's the first path: send money to one contact, or also request money and pay a bill? Does that match what you have in mind?
card.then: Wait for the interviewer to confirm the scope.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer asks about stored balance vs. a real bank/card behind the wallet, and proposes a concrete MVP path (send money to one contact), while also clarifying users and additional paths.
judge.criterion: SAY asks clarifying questions about scope (stored balance vs external rail, currency, offline behaviour, authority of the ledger) and proposes one MVP path such as send money to a contact.

turns.name: W2-design
turns.question: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees", "Balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads offline; submitting money needs network", "Server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope", "A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: requirements given, draw client/server/storage flowchart
card.say: Thanks, that's clear. So the MVP is one path: A sends 80 dollars to B, and B's balance goes from 0 to 80 dollars while A goes from 100 to 20.
card.type: draw@wallet design: flowchart TD ⏎     UI[Compose screens] --> VM[ViewModel] ⏎     VM --> Repo[Repository] ⏎     Repo --> DB[(Room cache)] ⏎     Repo --> API[API client] ⏎     API --> Srv[Wallet server] ⏎     Srv --> Ledger[(Ledger DB)]
card.then: I'll walk through each box and what it owns.

more: The board already shows the shape, so let me say what each part owns. The Compose screens only show state and send user actions. The ViewModel holds the screen state and calls the repository. The repository is the one place the UI reads from: it reads the Room cache first, then refreshes from the API client. The Room cache keeps the last balance and history, so reads work offline.

diagram.type: draw@wallet design: flowchart TD ⏎     UI[Compose screens] --> VM[ViewModel] ⏎

judge.detail: PASS: The mermaid flowchart includes UI, ViewModel, Repository, Room cache, API client, server, and ledger, and the SAY covers what the client parts own (screens show state/send actions, ViewModel holds state, repository reads cache then API, Room cache enables offline reads) plus the server ledger as authority.
judge.criterion: TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of the Android client (UI, ViewModel, repository, local database), the server and its ledger; SAY says what each part owns and that the server ledger is the authority.

turns.name: W2-seq
turns.question: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees", "Balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads offline; submitting money needs network", "Server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope", "A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars
card.say: I'll draw the send path from confirmation to the result screen. A confirms on the native screen, and the app sends one request with a client transfer ID. The server checks the balance and moves the money in one transaction. Then the app shows the result from the server's record.
card.type: draw@Compose screens: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as A's app ⏎     participant S as Wallet server ⏎     participant L as Ledger DB ⏎     A->>A: Confirm send 80 to B ⏎     A->>S: POST transfer, id T1, 8000 cents ⏎     S->>L: Check A has 100, then debit and credit ⏎     L-->>S: Committed, A 20, B 80 ⏎     S-->>A: T1 success ⏎     A->>A: Result screen shows success
card.then: Next, I'd cover the timeout case, where the app doesn't know yet.

more: The sequence is on the board now. The key point is the lost response. A timeout is not a failure, it's an unknown outcome. So the app asks the server about T1 again, and the server returns the same result for the same ID. The app shows success only from the server's record.

diagram.type: draw@Compose screens: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as A's app ⏎     parti

judge.detail: PASS: The diagram covers confirmation, POST with client transfer ID T1, atomic server debit/credit, response, and result screen; SAY states amounts in cents (8000) and final balances (A 20, B 80) and the result state.
judge.criterion: TYPE is a mermaid sequenceDiagram covering confirm, submit with a client transfer ID, an atomic server debit and credit, the response and the result; SAY covers amounts in cents and the final balances (A 20 dollars, B 80) and the result states.

turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the app sends "one request with a client transfer ID" — walk me through what's stored locally on Android before that request goes out, and what the result screen shows while the outcome is still unknown.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees", "Balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads offline; submitting money needs network", "Server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope", "A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: what's stored locally before the request, and what the result screen shows while unknown
card.say: Before the request goes out, I write one row in Room: transfer ID T1, amount 8000 cents, recipient B, and status pending. The result screen reads that row, so it shows "processing" and never a success. When the outcome is unknown, it says "still checking" and keeps the same T1. It only shows success when the server's record for T1 says success.
card.then: Next, I'd cover what happens if the app is killed while T1 is still pending.

more: The row also stores the time I sent it and a retry count, so the app can back off instead of hammering the server. And the result screen has a "Check again" button, so the user can ask for the status without sending a new transfer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer specifies the local Room row (T1, 8000 cents, recipient B, pending status) and the result screen's "processing"/"still checking" states, which directly addresses the card's prompt and is consistent with the earlier SSE/StateFlow and server-authoritative-ledger answers; it adds specifics (timestamp, retry count, "Check again" button) without inventing any employer, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W3-change1
turns.question: Your sequence shows "S-->>A: T1 success" and then "Result screen shows success," which assumes the response arrives. Now the server commits but the response is lost and Android kills the process before A reopens the app — what changes in your local storage and on relaunch? Please update your sequence diagram.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees", "Balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads offline; submitting money needs network", "Server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope", "A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: server commits, response lost, process killed before relaunch — update the sequence
card.say: Nothing new is stored, because the pending row for T1 was already written before the request went out. On relaunch, the app reads that row and sees T1 is still pending. So it doesn't send a new transfer. It calls GET transfer T1, and the server returns the committed record: A 20, B 80. Only then does the row become success and the result screen show it.
card.type: replace@A->>A: Result screen shows success: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as A's app ⏎     participant S as Wallet server ⏎     A->>A: Process killed, relaunch ⏎     A->>A: Read Room row T1, still pending ⏎     A->>S: GET transfer T1 ⏎     S-->>A: T1 success, A 20, B 80 ⏎     A->>A: Update row to success, show result
card.then: Next: what the row keeps if the lookup itself fails, and how long the app keeps checking.

more: Nothing new needs to be stored, because the pending row for T1 was already written before the request went out. On relaunch the app reads that row, sees T1 is still pending, and doesn't send a new transfer. It calls GET transfer T1, and the server returns the committed record: A 20, B 80. Only then does the row become success and the result screen show it.

diagram.type: replace@A->>A: Result screen shows success: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A

judge.detail: PASS: The answer treats the lost response as unknown (pending row, no new transfer), persists T1 before sending, queries the server by T1 after relaunch, and shows success only from the server's committed record — no new ID, one ledger transfer.
judge.criterion: SAY and TYPE treat the outcome as unknown (not failed), persist the transfer intent ID before sending, query the server by account and that ID after restart, and replay the same intent only if the server's idempotency contract allows; the server returns the original transfer's status for a repeat of the same ID; never a new ID; ledger has one transfer.

turns.name: W3-dyn
turns.question: You said relaunch calls GET transfer T1 and only then flips the row to success — what does the result screen show if that lookup comes back not found, since the row still says pending?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees", "Balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads offline; submitting money needs network", "Server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope", "A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: what does the result screen show if the lookup comes back not found
card.say: Not found doesn't prove the money didn't move. The request may still be in flight, or the read may lag behind the ledger. So the row stays pending, and the screen keeps saying "still checking". It never shows success or failure from a missing record. I'd keep checking with backoff, and after a set time show "we're still confirming, check again later" with a support path.
card.type: draw@the process-killed sequence diagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as A's app ⏎     participant S as Wallet server ⏎     A->>S: GET transfer T1 ⏎     S-->>A: Not found ⏎     A->>A: Row stays pending, show still checking ⏎     A->>S: Retry GET T1 with backoff
card.then: Next: how long the app keeps checking, and what the user sees after that.

more: The screen keeps the same four states: success, clear failure, processing, and outcome unknown. Not found is not a failure, so it stays on "still checking". I'd also show one line under it: "If this takes longer, contact support with transfer ID T1." That gives the user something to do while we keep checking.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer correctly treats "not found" as an unknown outcome rather than failure, keeps the row pending with "still checking," adds specific new detail (backoff, support path with transfer ID T1), and stays consistent with the earlier pending-row/GET-T1 design without inventing any new wallet rules or credentials.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W4-concurrency
turns.question: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP user path
card.constraints: ["Signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal P2P transfers, zero fees", "Balance, transfer, history and details in scope; cached reads offline; submitting money needs network", "Server owns the authoritative ledger and limits; top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency out of scope", "A has 100 dollars, B has 0"]
card.heard: two phones, two independent 80 dollar transfers at the same time
card.say: Only one can succeed. The server checks A's balance and debits it in one transaction, so the first request locks A's row and takes A from 100 to 20. The second request waits, then sees only 20 dollars left, so it fails with "not enough balance". On the phones, the first one shows success with A 20 and B 80. The second shows a clear failure, and B's balance goes to 80, not 160.
card.then: Next: what the second phone shows if its response is lost, and how the user retries safely.

more: The second phone also refreshes A's balance from the server, so the user sees 20 dollars, not 100. It shows a clear failure: not enough balance. The row for that second transfer ID stays failed, and no money moves. So the two phones never disagree, because both read the server's ledger.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer treats the two transfers as independent intents, has the server check and debit A's balance in one transaction with a row lock, makes the first succeed and the second fail for insufficient balance, and ends A at 20 dollars.
judge.criterion: SAY treats them as two intents with separate IDs, checks and debits the balance in one transaction (row lock or conditional update), one succeeds and one fails for insufficient funds, A ends at 20 dollars.

turns.name: W5-account
turns.question: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?

card.problem: Tell about a delivery risk where the team disagreed: when I told whom, options, who decided, what I finished
card.heard: account switched to C, old response arrives
card.say: The danger is that A's old response lands while C is on screen. So C could see A's balance or a success message for A's transfer. I'd tag every request and callback with the account and a session generation. When a response comes back, I check the session first. If it's no longer current, I drop it and don't write it to the UI.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer scopes UI updates to account and session generation, drops stale callbacks so C never sees A's data, and prevents cross-account leakage; it does not claim A's committed transfer is lost (recovery via A's history is implied by server-authoritative ledger and pending-row reconciliation), and it says nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY scopes cache writes and UI to account and session, drops callbacks from a stale session, C never sees A's data, and A's committed transfer is recovered from A's history after A signs in again.

turns.name: W6-change2
turns.question: You said the row stays pending and the screen keeps saying "still checking" — now the pilot also starts from a group chat with "pay Alex for last night's dinner," two contacts named Alex, no reliable amount, and the chat stream disconnects right after confirm. What changes in your flow, and what does the user see? And right after the user confirms, the chat stream disconnects. Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.

card.problem: Tell about a delivery risk where the team disagreed: when I told whom, options, who decided, what I finished
card.constraints: ["Pilot entry from a group chat: \'pay Alex for last night\'s dinner\', two contacts named Alex, no reliable amount, chat stream disconnects right after confirm"]
card.heard: New entry flow: group chat, two Alexes, no amount, stream drops after confirm
card.say: Two things change. The chat only suggests the payment; the money is still authorized on our native confirm screen, with the payer, the recipient and the amount bound to one transfer ID. With two Alexes and no reliable amount, the assistant must ask and show both matches, and it never guesses. If the chat stream drops after confirm, the payment still goes ahead, because it doesn't depend on the chat. The user sees "processing" from the pending row, and the result comes from the server's record.
card.type: draw@new entry flow: flowchart TD ⏎     Chat[Group chat message] --> Asst[Assistant suggests payment] ⏎     Asst --> Ask[Ask: which Alex, what amount] ⏎     Ask --> Confirm[Native confirm screen] ⏎     Confirm --> Row[(Room row T1 pending)] ⏎     Row --> API[API client] ⏎     API --> Srv[Wallet server] ⏎     Srv --> Ledger[(Ledger DB)] ⏎     Srv --> Result[Result screen from server record]
card.then: Next: what the confirm screen shows when the chat stream is already gone.

more: The payment doesn't wait for the chat. The confirm screen already wrote the pending row for T1, so the transfer goes ahead on its own. When the chat reconnects, it reads that row and tells the user the payment is already done. It doesn't offer a second payment.

diagram.type: draw@new entry flow: flowchart TD ⏎     Chat[Group chat message] --> Asst[Assist

judge.detail: PASS: The answer covers asking which Alex and what amount, a native confirm screen binding payer/recipient/amount to one transfer ID, the payment proceeding independently when the chat drops, and status from the server's record; it states the assistant never guesses and the chat only suggests, so the model never authorizes.
judge.criterion: SAY asks the user which Alex and what amount, shows a trusted native confirmation with recipient and amount, binds authorization to those parameters server-side, ties a repeated tool call to the original intent, and recovers status from the payment service when the chat drops; the model never authorizes. TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of that entry flow.

turns.name: W6-dyn
turns.question: You said the assistant "never guesses" and the amount is bound to one transfer ID on the native confirm screen — so what happens if the recipient changes after that confirmation, say the chat later resolves to the other Alex?

card.problem: Tell about a delivery risk where the team disagreed: when I told whom, options, who decided, what I finished
card.constraints: ["Pilot entry from a group chat: \'pay Alex for last night\'s dinner\', two contacts named Alex, no reliable amount, chat stream disconnects right after confirm"]
card.heard: recipient changes after confirmation
card.say: The confirmation is the authorization, so the recipient is locked to T1. If the chat later resolves to the other Alex, that's a new payment, not a change to T1. The app shows the confirmed recipient and amount on the result screen, and the server rejects any request that changes them for T1. If the user really wants the other Alex, they cancel nothing and start a new transfer with a new ID, and the first one still finishes on its own.
card.type: draw@: flowchart TD ⏎     Confirm -->|binds payer, recipient, amount to T1| Lock[Server rejects T1 with a different recipient] ⏎     Chat -->|resolves to other Alex| New[New transfer, new ID T2]
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer builds directly on the candidate's own prior statements (confirmation as authorization, recipient/amount bound to T1, server-owned ledger, new ID for a new payment), adds specific new detail (server rejects T1 with a changed recipient, result screen shows confirmed recipient/amount, first transfer finishes on its own), stays consistent with the earlier flow (pending row, server record, no double payment), and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule beyond what was given.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W7-release

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The users were travelers on the KKday app.
Candidate: Planning a trip by hand was slow: they worked out the budget, searched products one by one, then put the plan together themselves.
Candidate: My responsibility started at the technical plan.
Candidate: I designed the agent, connected it to our product and order data, and built the core backend.
Candidate: It ended at the Android side of the result.
Interviewer: On the KKday agent project, you said your responsibility "ended at the Android side" — so which exact pieces did you build yourself versus the team?
Candidate: I built the agent design and the core backend myself.
Candidate: That covers the tools for product and order data, the personalization data layer, and the checks with retry and fallback.
Candidate: On Android, I wrote the code that reads the SSE stream of the trip plan.
Candidate: The app team built the other screens, like the day cards and the map.
Candidate: The project had five people, and I was the technical lead.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made myself is the Android side of the trip plan stream.
Candidate: A user types "Tokyo, 5,000 yuan, 3 days" and taps plan.
Candidate: The app opens the SSE connection and reads each event as it arrives.
Candidate: I parse each event into a day card and post it to a StateFlow, so the screen shows day one while the rest is still coming.
Candidate: The logic I changed is the parsing and the state update, not the screens.
Candidate: The parsing runs on a background dispatcher, so the main thread only updates the UI.
Candidate: Each event is checked before it becomes a card.
Candidate: If one event is bad, I skip it and keep the rest of the plan.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest one was a plan that looked fine but showed the wrong day order.
Candidate: I first suspected the stream itself, so I logged every event as it arrived.
Candidate: The log showed the events came in order, so the stream was fine.
Candidate: The real cause was my own parsing: I keyed the cards by arrival, not by the day number in the event.
Candidate: So a late retry from the backend put day two above day one.
Interviewer: You said a late retry from the backend put day two above day one — how did you confirm that was the actual cause rather than just a plausible story?
Candidate: I reproduced it on purpose.
Candidate: I sent the same plan again with a late day-two event, and the cards came out in the wrong order every time.
Candidate: Then I changed the key to the day number, and the same replay came out in order.
Candidate: That proved it was my parsing, not the stream.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: There were two other options.
Candidate: First, I could sort the cards on the screen after each update.
Candidate: That works, but the list jumps around while the user is reading.
Candidate: Second, I could ask the backend to send the days in order and wait for the full plan.
Candidate: That's slower, and a late retry can still arrive out of order.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At KKday, close to a release, I found that some old pages broke the back button with the new navigation.
Candidate: I hadn't checked every page yet, but it could already affect the release.
Candidate: I told the project manager that same day.
Candidate: I gave two options: keep the old pages and move my change to the next release, or ship it and accept the risk.
Candidate: He decided to move my change.

Interviewer: You said the PM chose to "move my change" rather than ship with the back-button risk — so what risk were you personally willing to accept before that release, and what signal afterward would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: Before that release, I was willing to accept one risk: the pages I hadn't checked yet might also break.
Candidate: So I said that clearly, and I asked for a quick way to turn the new navigation off.
Candidate: After release, I watched the crash reports and the back-button errors in Bugly.
Candidate: If the number went up, I'd pause the change and keep the old pages working.
Candidate: Then I'd own the fix and the retest, and we'd ship it again when the errors were gone.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Before I design anything, I'd like to confirm a few things.
Candidate: Who are the users: friends sending money to each other, or a business paying customers?
Candidate: Where does the money actually live: a real bank or card behind the wallet, or a stored balance we hold ourselves?
Candidate: And what's the first path: send money to one contact, or also request money and pay a bill?
Candidate: Does that match what you have in mind?

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.
Candidate: Thanks, that's clear.
Candidate: So the MVP is one path: A sends 80 dollars to B, and B's balance goes from 0 to 80 dollars while A goes from 100 to 20.

[board] flowchart TD |     UI[Compose screens] --> VM[ViewModel] |     VM --> Repo[Repository] |     Repo --> DB[(Room cache)] |     Repo --> API[API client] |     API --> Srv[Wallet server] |     Srv --> Ledger[(Ledger DB)]
Candidate: The board already shows the shape, so let me say what each part owns.
Candidate: The Compose screens only show state and send user actions.
Candidate: The ViewModel holds the screen state and calls the repository.
Candidate: The repository is the one place the UI reads from: it reads the Room cache first, then refreshes from the API client.
Candidate: The Room cache keeps the last balance and history, so reads work offline.
Interviewer: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: I'll draw the send path from confirmation to the result screen.
Candidate: A confirms on the native screen, and the app sends one request with a client transfer ID.
Candidate: The server checks the balance and moves the money in one transaction.
Candidate: Then the app shows the result from the server's record.

[board] sequenceDiagram |     participant A as A's app |     participant S as Wallet server |     participant L as Ledger DB |     A->>A: Confirm send 80 to B |     A->>S: POST transfer, id T1, 8000 cents |     S->>L: Check A has 100, then debit and credit |     L-->>S: Committed, A 20, B 80 |     S-->>A: T1 success |     A->>A: Result screen shows success
Candidate: The sequence is on the board now.
Candidate: The key point is the lost response.
Candidate: A timeout is not a failure, it's an unknown outcome.
Candidate: So the app asks the server about T1 again, and the server returns the same result for the same ID.
Candidate: The app shows success only from the server's record.

Interviewer: You said the app sends "one request with a client transfer ID" — walk me through what's stored locally on Android before that request goes out, and what the result screen shows while the outcome is still unknown.
Candidate: Before the request goes out, I write one row in Room: transfer ID T1, amount 8000 cents, recipient B, and status pending.
Candidate: The result screen reads that row, so it shows "processing" and never a success.
Candidate: When the outcome is unknown, it says "still checking" and keeps the same T1.
Candidate: It only shows success when the server's record for T1 says success.
Candidate: The row also stores the time I sent it and a retry count, so the app can back off instead of hammering the server.
Candidate: And the result screen has a "Check again" button, so the user can ask for the status without sending a new transfer.

Interviewer: Your sequence shows "S-->>A: T1 success" and then "Result screen shows success," which assumes the response arrives. Now the server commits but the response is lost and Android kills the process before A reopens the app — what changes in your local storage and on relaunch? Please update your sequence diagram.
Candidate: Nothing new is stored, because the pending row for T1 was already written before the request went out.
Candidate: On relaunch, the app reads that row and sees T1 is still pending.
Candidate: So it doesn't send a new transfer.
Candidate: It calls GET transfer T1, and the server returns the committed record: A 20, B 80.
Candidate: Only then does the row become success and the result screen show it.

[board] Result screen shows success: sequenceDiagram |     participant A as A's app |     participant S as Wallet server |     A->>A: Process killed, relaunch |     A->>A: Read Room row T1, still pending |     A->>S: GET transfer T1 |     S-->>A: T1 success, A 20, B 80 |     A->>A: Update row to success, show result
Candidate: Nothing new needs to be stored, because the pending row for T1 was already written before the request went out.
Candidate: On relaunch the app reads that row, sees T1 is still pending, and doesn't send a new transfer.
Candidate: It calls GET transfer T1, and the server returns the committed record: A 20, B 80.
Candidate: Only then does the row become success and the result screen show it.
Interviewer: You said relaunch calls GET transfer T1 and only then flips the row to success — what does the result screen show if that lookup comes back not found, since the row still says pending?
Candidate: Not found doesn't prove the money didn't move.
Candidate: The request may still be in flight, or the read may lag behind the ledger.
Candidate: So the row stays pending, and the screen keeps saying "still checking".
Candidate: It never shows success or failure from a missing record.
Candidate: I'd keep checking with backoff, and after a set time show "we're still confirming, check again later" with a support path.

[board] sequenceDiagram |     participant A as A's app |     participant S as Wallet server |     A->>S: GET transfer T1 |     S-->>A: Not found |     A->>A: Row stays pending, show still checking |     A->>S: Retry GET T1 with backoff
Candidate: The screen keeps the same four states: success, clear failure, processing, and outcome unknown.
Candidate: Not found is not a failure, so it stays on "still checking".
Candidate: I'd also show one line under it: "If this takes longer, contact support with transfer ID T1." That gives the user something to do while we keep checking.

Interviewer: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?
Candidate: Only one can succeed.
Candidate: The server checks A's balance and debits it in one transaction, so the first request locks A's row and takes A from 100 to 20.
Candidate: The second request waits, then sees only 20 dollars left, so it fails with "not enough balance".
Candidate: On the phones, the first one shows success with A 20 and B 80.
Candidate: The second shows a clear failure, and B's balance goes to 80, not 160.
Candidate: The second phone also refreshes A's balance from the server, so the user sees 20 dollars, not 100.
Candidate: It shows a clear failure: not enough balance.
Candidate: The row for that second transfer ID stays failed, and no money moves.
Candidate: So the two phones never disagree, because both read the server's ledger.
Interviewer: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?
Candidate: The danger is that A's old response lands while C is on screen.
Candidate: So C could see A's balance or a success message for A's transfer.
Candidate: I'd tag every request and callback with the account and a session generation.
Candidate: When a response comes back, I check the session first.
Candidate: If it's no longer current, I drop it and don't write it to the UI.

Interviewer: You said the row stays pending and the screen keeps saying "still checking" — now the pilot also starts from a group chat with "pay Alex for last night's dinner," two contacts named Alex, no reliable amount, and the chat stream disconnects right after confirm. What changes in your flow, and what does the user see? And right after the user confirms, the chat stream disconnects. Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.
Candidate: Two things change.
Candidate: The chat only suggests the payment; the money is still authorized on our native confirm screen, with the payer, the recipient and the amount bound to one transfer ID.
Candidate: With two Alexes and no reliable amount, the assistant must ask and show both matches, and it never guesses.
Candidate: If the chat stream drops after confirm, the payment still goes ahead, because it doesn't depend on the chat.
Candidate: The user sees "processing" from the pending row, and the result comes from the server's record.

[board] flowchart TD |     Chat[Group chat message] --> Asst[Assistant suggests payment] |     Asst --> Ask[Ask: which Alex, what amount] |     Ask --> Confirm[Native confirm screen] |     Confirm --> Row[(Room row T1 pending)] |     Row --> API[API client] |     API --> Srv[Wallet server] |     Srv --> Ledger[(Ledger DB)] |     Srv --> Result[Result screen from server record]
Candidate: The payment doesn't wait for the chat.
Candidate: The confirm screen already wrote the pending row for T1, so the transfer goes ahead on its own.
Candidate: When the chat reconnects, it reads that row and tells the user the payment is already done.
Candidate: It doesn't offer a second payment.

Interviewer: You said the assistant "never guesses" and the amount is bound to one transfer ID on the native confirm screen — so what happens if the recipient changes after that confirmation, say the chat later resolves to the other Alex?
Candidate: The confirmation is the authorization, so the recipient is locked to T1.
Candidate: If the chat later resolves to the other Alex, that's a new payment, not a change to T1.
Candidate: The app shows the confirmed recipient and amount on the result screen, and the server rejects any request that changes them for T1.
Candidate: If the user really wants the other Alex, they cancel nothing and start a new transfer with a new ID, and the first one still finishes on its own.
[board] flowchart TD |     Confirm -->|binds payer, recipient, amount to T1| Lock[Server rejects T1 with a different recipient] |     Chat -->|resolves to other Alex| New[New transfer, new ID T2]

Interviewer: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?
Candidate: Two weeks is enough for one path: send to one contact, with the pending row, the status lookup and the four result states.
Candidate: Login and the ledger already exist, so I'd skip history filters and polish.
Candidate: The tech lead signs off on the API contract, and product signs off on the four result states.
Candidate: If pending transfers spike, I'd first check whether it's real money stuck or just slow status reads.
Candidate: Then I'd pause new sends, keep reads and status working, and reconcile every pending T1 with the ledger before we resume.

[board] flowchart TD |     Send[Send to one contact] --> Row[(Room row T1 pending)] |     Row --> API[API client] |     API --> Srv[Wallet server] |     Srv --> Ledger[(Ledger DB)] |     Srv --> Result[Result screen: four states]
Candidate: The cap is a guard, not a number I'd guess.
Candidate: I'd set it from how fast we can reconcile one pending T1 by hand.
Candidate: If the spike is real stuck money, the cap pauses sends before the backlog gets too big to clear in one sitting.

Interviewer: You said you'd pause new sends and reconcile every pending T1 before resuming — in that half hour, what do you personally own versus hand off, who do you need in the room, and at what point do you escalate to me?
Candidate: I own the client side: the pending rows, the status lookups and what the result screen shows.
Candidate: I'd hand the ledger reconciliation to the backend on-call, because the ledger is theirs.
Candidate: In the room I need the backend on-call, the tech lead and product.
Candidate: I'd escalate to you once we know whether real money is stuck, and give you the count and the plan.
Candidate: If we can't tell within the half hour, I'd escalate anyway.
Interviewer: That's it from me. What questions do you have for me about the team or the role?
Candidate: Yes, I have two.
Candidate: First, six months after I join, what would make you feel you hired the right Android engineer?
Candidate: Second, what's the biggest mobile challenge right now: voice response speed, handling partial results, or reliable actions?
